name: Celtic torc

lead: A torc is a large, stiff neck ring, usually of gold or bronze, worn across Europe from the late Bronze Age through the Iron Age. Among the Celts it signalled high rank and wealth. As jewellery it gives a bold, structured line around the neck and is used today as a historical or heritage-style accessory.
Its appearance effect is a styling one: it draws attention to the neck and shoulders and suits open collars. Nothing about it is clinical, and no studies look at its use.

paras: A torc sits around the neck, open at the front or fastened with a hook-and-ring or locking catch. Modern torc-style jewellery is made in metals such as bronze, brass, silver or gold-plated alloys, and is worn with open-necked clothing, costume or reenactment kit.

A rigid ring can be uncomfortable if it does not fit the neck. Many ancient torcs were designed for near-permanent wear and were difficult to remove, a point that does not apply to modern replicas with clasps. Some people react to nickel or other alloys in costume metals.

chain: Rigid metal ring worn at the neck
Draws the eye to neck and shoulder line
angle.text: A torc is a visible neck accessory. It adds a defined metallic line around the neck and is worn with open collars to add presence.

lead: A torc (also spelled torque) is a large rigid or stiff neck ring in metal, often twisted, from the Latin word for twist. Most open at the front, though some use hook-and-ring closures or locking catches [1].

As a piece of adornment, the torc frames the neck and collarbone line and carries strong visual and status associations. In the Iron Age it marked rank among Celtic peoples; today it is worn as heritage jewellery, in costume and in reenactment.
Torcs are archaeological and historical objects and are not the subject of clinical research.
infobox: Gold, bronze, less often silver or iron
From c. 1200 BC; common 8th century BC to 3rd century AD
Vix torc, Snettisham Torc, Broighter Gold, Stirling Hoard

paras: Torcs were made from single rods or from twisted strands, mostly in gold or bronze, which survive burial better than other metals. Some were made in silver, iron or other metals [1]. Many were designed for near-permanent wear and would have been hard to remove [1].

Rigid gold and bronze neck rings appear in the later European Bronze Age from around 1200 BC. Torcs were common in Iron Age cultures from the 8th century BC to the 3rd century AD, worn by Scythian, Illyrian, Thracian and Celtic peoples. Celtic torcs disappear in the Migration Period, and torc-style silver necklaces return in the Viking Age [1].

Among the Celts the torc marked high rank. Early Celtic torcs are mostly found with women until the 3rd century BC, after which they are mostly, though not exclusively, associated with men. Gods such as Cernunnos are depicted wearing them [1].

Famous finds include the Vix torc from France (c. 480 BC), the Snettisham Torc from Norfolk, a 1st-century BC electrum piece containing about a kilogram of gold, the Broighter Gold from Ireland and the Stirling Hoard from Scotland [1]. Roman writers recorded torcs as war trophies: Titus Manlius Torquatus took his nickname from the torc of a Gaul he killed in 361 BC, and Polybius described Gaesatae warriors at Telamon (225 BC) as naked except for torcs [1].

Torc-style jewellery is sold as costume, historical-reenactment and heritage pieces. Wikipedia's account of the topic does not discuss modern revivals, so the extent of its use in looksmaxxing or appearance communities is not documented here.
